idiom_name: class composition + AutoCloseable/try-with-resources (Cleaner as safety net)
implementation_notes: A Java whole is a class whose fields are its parts; the JVM reclaims memory nondeterministically, so every part that holds a resource must be released deterministically instead: the whole implements AutoCloseable, its close() cascades to the parts it owns, and callers scope it with try-with-resources. finalize() is deprecated for removal, and Oracle's guidance replaces it with either try-with-resources (resources confined to a scope) or java.lang.ref.Cleaner (a backstop for objects that outlive any scope), whose cleaning action must be a static state object that does not reference the cleaned instance. The explicit Whole class remains the right shape when parts are created, replaced and removed at runtime behind a stable interface; for immutable data, plain composition of final fields is enough.
pitfalls: A cleaning action (including a lambda) that captures the whole keeps it phantom-reachable, so the Cleaner never fires - keep the state in a static nested class.
Returning the live parts list or leaking element references lets callers mutate parts behind the whole; return List.copyOf, streams or domain queries instead.
close() must be idempotent and must cascade only to owned parts: a closed whole that is used again should fail fast (IllegalStateException) rather than operate on released resources.
